question: In a jaundiced neonate, an elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin fraction greater than 1 mg/dL or greater than 20% of the total serum bilirubin is always abnormal and indicates a pathological cause such as cholestasis, biliary atresia, or sepsis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. The statement is TRUE. Unlike indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin — which is common and physiological in the first week — conjugated (direct) bilirubin is NEVER normal in neonates. Any conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia mandates urgent evaluation for biliary atresia (which requires Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy before 60 days of age for best outcomes), neonatal hepatitis, or metabolic/infectious causes.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! Direct bilirubin is NEVER physiological in any neonate. Any elevation of conjugated bilirubin (>1 mg/dL or >20% TSB) is a red flag for serious underlying pathology: biliary atresia (a surgical emergency if not diagnosed by 6–8 weeks), neonatal hepatitis (TORCH infections), choledochal cyst, Alagille syndrome, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, or neonatal sepsis. All such infants require urgent investigation including USS abdomen and hepatobiliary scintigraphy.
